parts.label: (a)
parts.text: By reference to the direction of propagation of energy, state what is meant by a transverse wave.

markscheme_points.text: vibrations / oscillations (of the particles / wave) are perpendicular to the direction (of the propagation of energy)

hints: Hint 1: Think of two different directions in a wave - the direction the particles or fields vibrate, and the direction the energy itself travels. How are these two directions lined up for a transverse wave compared to a longitudinal wave?
parts.proper_answer: A transverse wave is one in which the vibrations or oscillations are perpendicular to the direction of propagation of energy.
walkthrough:
Step 1: **Picture What Oscillates and What Travels**
Imagine a rope shaken up and down. Each bit of rope moves up and down, but the wave pulse and its energy travel along the rope. So you always have two directions to compare.

Step 2: **Define Transverse Clearly**
For a transverse wave those two directions are at 90 degrees to each other. In symbols, if energy propagates along $x$, oscillation is along $y$ or $z$. All electromagnetic waves are transverse.

parts.label: (b)
parts.text:
A space telescope is designed to detect electromagnetic radiation with wavelengths in the range $12\,\mu\text{m}$ to $28\,\mu\text{m}$.

State the region of the electromagnetic spectrum for this radiation.
hints: Hint 1: Convert the wavelengths to metres in your head - $1 \, \mu\text{m} = 10^{-6} \, \text{m}$ - and recall where visible light sits at about $0.4$ to $0.7 \, \mu\text{m}$. Is $12$ to $28 \, \mu\text{m}$ shorter or longer than visible light?
walkthrough:
Step 1: **Place 12 to 28 Micrometre on the Spectrum**
$12 \, \mu\text{m} = 12 \times 10^{-6} \, \text{m}$ and $28 \, \mu\text{m} = 28 \times 10^{-6} \, \text{m}$. Visible light is roughly $0.40 \times 10^{-6} \, \text{m}$ to $0.70 \times 10^{-6} \, \text{m}$.

Step 2: **Identify the Neighbouring Region**
Wavelengths longer than red light but shorter than microwaves ($\sim 10^{-3} \, \text{m}$) belong to the infrared region. So this space telescope is an infrared telescope.

parts.label: (c)
parts.text:
A detector on another space telescope detects an electromagnetic wave. The signal from the detector is transmitted to Earth and displayed on an oscilloscope as shown in Fig. 5.1. The frequency of the signal displayed on the oscilloscope is equal to the frequency of the detected electromagnetic wave.

{{figure:figure_5_1}}

The time-base setting on the oscilloscope is $5.0 \times 10^{-15} \text{s cm}^{-1}$.

Calculate the wavelength of the detected electromagnetic wave.
hints: Hint 1: Look along the horizontal time axis in Fig. 5.1 and count how many centimetres wide one complete cycle of the sine wave is - for example from one rising zero-crossing to the next rising zero-crossing.

Hint 2: The time-base tells you what each centimetre means in seconds. Think how you combine the width of one cycle with the $5.0 \times 10^{-15} \, \text{s cm}^{-1}$ setting to get the time period $T$.
Hint 3: Once you have the period, you have the frequency from $f = 1/T$. Recall the universal wave speed for all electromagnetic waves in space and how it links $c$, $f$ and $\lambda$.
walkthrough:
Step 1: **Find the Length of One Period on the Screen**
You are looking at voltage against time, so horizontal distance is time. One full sine wave repeats after 6.0 cm. You can see this, for example, from the zero crossing going up at about 1 cm to the next zero crossing going up at about 7 cm. So:
$$ \text{width of one cycle} = 6.0 \, \text{cm} $$

Step 2: **Convert Screen Width to Time Period**
The time-base is $5.0 \times 10^{-15} \, \text{s cm}^{-1}$, meaning each 1.0 cm is $5.0 \times 10^{-15} \, \text{s}$. Multiply:
$$ T = 6.0 \times 5.0 \times 10^{-15} \, \text{s} $$
$$ T = 3.0 \times 10^{-14} \, \text{s} $$
This is also the period of the detected electromagnetic wave, because the displayed frequency equals the wave frequency.

Step 3: **Use the Wave Equation for Light**
All electromagnetic waves in free space travel at $c = 3.0 \times 10^{8} \, \text{m s}^{-1}$. Use:
$$ c = f\lambda = \frac{\lambda}{T} $$
$$ \lambda = cT $$
$$ \lambda = 3.0 \times 10^{8} \times 3.0 \times 10^{-14} $$
$$ \lambda = 9.0 \times 10^{-6} \, \text{m} $$
That is $9.0 \, \mu\text{m}$, consistent with infrared radiation.
